title: 'I drew my firearm to protect myself from being stabbed'
article: Const. Mike Sibley and Douglas Heagle had crossed paths prior to their fatal encounter in 2009.
Speaking at a coroner's inquest in Midland Tuesday, the Midland police officer recounted two other occasions he had been to the Scott Street residence Heagle shared with his mother Betty Heagle.
"I had previous dealings with Douglas under the Mental Health Act," Sibley told the five-member jury.

Sibley recalled being dispatched to the Heagle residence following Betty Heagle's 911 call on Feb. 3, 2009. He also spoke of the events that led to Douglas Heagle, 38, dying less than an hour later at Georgian Bay General Hospital from a single gunshot wound.

After arriving at the home that day, Sibley said, he spoke with Betty Heagle, "who seemed timid and scared" and was waiting outside. He asked her if there were any weapons in the home, and inquired about her son's mental illness and whether he was taking his medication.
"In the house, I could hear loud mumbling, but nothing was making sense," Sibley testified, noting he opened a side door and soon came face-to-face with Heagle.
"Douglas was staring down at me with knives in both hands. I yelled 'knives' to let my partners know, and immediately created a space between Douglas and I."
Sibley said the initial five-foot space between them gradually collapsed to three feet and continued to get smaller.
At that point, with Heagle continuing to move toward him and backed up against a snowbank with no way out, Sibley said he drew his firearm and fired a single shot.

"When Douglas was still in possession of multiple knives in each hand, I drew my firearm to protect myself from being stabbed," Sibley said. "I told Douglas to drop the knives and get down on the ground multiple times.
"He just turned, looked at me. There was nothing there. He was just staring at me."
Sibley said Heagle was conscious after the shooting and asked if he had been hit with a Taser weapon.

The inquest, which is expected to wrap up Friday, is examining the circumstances surrounding Heagle's death. After all evidence and witnesses have been heard, the jury is empowered to make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
As a supervisor, retired Sgt. Doug Geffros carried a Taser. But Geffros, who was also at the scene, told jurors via a video recording that Sibley had no choice but to fire his weapon.

"He had no other option. (Heagle) was only about two feet from him when he shot," said Geffros, adding events escalated so quickly that he wouldn't have had time to remove and use his Taser, which delivers a jolt of electricity to subdue a suspect.

Const. Tyler Kukkonen also responded to the scene that February day, and was in the home's basement when he heard Sibley's shouts. He said he yelled for Heagle to stop and drop his weapon, but got no response.
Following the shooting, Kukkonen returned to his cruiser to retrieve crime-scene tape and a blanket for Heagle.
Const. Dawson Smith also testified Sibley had no choice but to shoot Heagle because of his "wild" behaviour that afternoon.
"Officer Sibley's life was in grave danger," Smith said, adding he handcuffed Heagle after the shooting and then comforted him, telling the injured man he would be all right.
"I told him you should drop your weapon when ordered to by police," Smith said. "Surprisingly, he answered me. He said, 'Yeah, you're right, I should have.'"
Sibley, who joined the Midland force in 2002, had also visited the Heagle home twice in 2004. The first time, on March 29, Heagle was "trashing" the modest bungalow he shared with his mother.

"He told me he was hearing voices calling him 'a faggot, a homo' and telling him he had AIDS," Sibley said, noting Heagle had been taken to hospital after a suspected suicide attempt from a pill overdose the week before.
Then, on New Year's Eve, Sibley again went to the home to find Heagle agitated and destroying property. That time, Heagle asked to be taken to hospital.

Psychiatrist Dr. Mara Goldstein reviewed Heagle's medical records following his death. She told jurors that, besides suffering from the effects of fetal alcohol syndrome, such as developmental delays and control issues, Heagle also experienced severe seizures along with a long history of depression and anxiety.
"He experienced voices in his head," said Goldstein, who pointed out Heagle had experienced success with his family doctor, who had retired by the time of the shooting.
"He had beliefs that his body was controlled by outside sources. He was not given the diagnosis of schizophrenia, but he had many of the symptoms."
And while Heagle took an assortment of prescription drugs, Goldstein said taking too much of the medications would have led to drowsiness, not aggression.
"Psychosis doesn't mean a person is dangerous," she said. "Many people (suffering through psychosis) live in our communities without incident.
"We don't have windows into the future.... I wish we did. The best prediction of behaviour is past behaviour."
